stemMd: The final paragraph implies that, once a single posted copy was accepted as notice to a whole city, the maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one could be used to
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: penalise heralds who had failed to read an ordinance at every station.

options.label: B
options.textMd: excuse a citizen who showed that the edict had not been posted in his own quarter.

options.label: C
options.textMd: hold a person bound by a rule that had never in fact come to his knowledge.

options.label: D
options.textMd: require the authority to prove that each citizen had actually read the edict.

explanationMd:
An implication question asks what the passage commits itself to without saying it in so many words. Here two sentences have to be put together.

The third paragraph says that courts began to accept "a single copy fixed to the door of the town hall as notice to the whole city" — so a citizen who never passed that door was treated as notified all the same. The final paragraph then says the maxim became "a rule about who must bear the cost when [the law] was not" carried to every door, and that the burden of knowing the law passed to "those who had to obey it."

Combine them. If a single posting counts as notice, a person who never saw it is still bound, and the maxim stops him from pleading his ignorance. That is what it means for the subject to "bear the cost": he can be held to a rule that never actually reached him.

**How to check.** Contrast the earlier world. Under proclamation, the maxim was "very nearly true" because ignorance had been made impossible; the passage's point is that in the later world ignorance was perfectly possible but no longer excused. The choice about holding a person bound by a rule that never came to his knowledge is the only one that describes that gap.

distractorRationale.b: This describes the earlier, medieval arrangement, in which a citizen could escape a penalty by showing that an ordinance had not been cried in his quarter. Once a single copy counted as notice to the whole city, there was no longer any per-quarter requirement to invoke.
distractorRationale.d: This is the reverse of the shift the passage describes. The burden moved away from the authority and onto the citizen, so the later maxim relieved the authority of proving anything beyond a single posting.
distractorRationale.a: Heralds belong to the earlier system that posting replaced, and the passage never discusses penalising them. The final paragraph is about the position of the citizens who must obey the law, not of officials.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying passage on the proclamation of laws. It asks what the final paragraph implies the maxim that ignorance of the law excuses no one could be used to do, once a single posted copy was accepted as notice to a whole city. The four answer options are: penalise heralds who had failed to read an ordinance at every station; excuse a citizen who showed that the edict had not been posted in his own quarter; hold a person bound by a rule that had never in fact come to his knowledge; require the authority to prove that each citizen had actually read the edict.
